body:
Why agriculture sustained both states

In both Vijayanagara and the Bahmani Sultanate, agriculture formed an essential economic foundation. Rulers and their officers depended on revenue from cultivated land to maintain armies, officials, forts and royal establishments.

Fertile river valleys were especially valuable because they supported agricultural production and settlement. Consequently, control over productive land was both an economic and a political objective. The recurring struggle for the Raichur Doab illustrates this relationship between agriculture, taxation and military power.

Water management and agricultural production

In the relatively dry environment around Vijayanagara, irrigation helped sustain agriculture and urban populations. The rulers supported the construction and maintenance of tanks, reservoirs and canals.

The Kamalapuram tank, constructed in the early 15th century, provided water for agricultural land and helped supply the royal centre. The Hiriya canal drew water from the Tungabhadra system and irrigated the cultivated area near the city.

These works were economically important. Improved water availability helped support cultivation, and successful agriculture supplied food to towns and armies while producing revenue for rulers and military commanders.

Why imported horses were valuable

Medieval warfare increasingly relied on effective cavalry. Rulers of Vijayanagara and the Deccan required strong, well-trained horses for military campaigns, and substantial numbers were imported from Arabia and Central Asia.

Arab merchants played a major role in supplying horses. Local merchants known as kudirai chettis, or horse traders, also participated. The competition to secure imported horses made coastal trade routes important to inland kingdoms.

From 1498, Portuguese traders and naval forces became increasingly influential on India's western coast. In 1510, the Portuguese captured Goa, which became a major Portuguese base. Their growing involvement in maritime trade and regional politics affected the kingdoms that depended on coastal commerce.

Ports and commercial routes

Ports on the western coast, including Goa and Dabhol, were strategically valuable because they connected the Deccan hinterland with maritime trade. Their political control changed over time, and they should not be treated as permanent possessions of one kingdom throughout the period.

Mahmud Gawan's western campaigns strengthened Bahmani access to coastal areas and important commercial centres. Vijayanagara likewise sought reliable access to merchants and imported goods, whether through directly controlled territories or commercial relationships.

The commercial economy included textiles, spices, precious stones, pearls and other valuable commodities. Vijayanagara's markets attracted merchants dealing in both luxury goods and ordinary provisions. The royal court's demand for valuable goods contributed to urban prosperity.

Trade, state policy and military strength

Krishnadeva Raya's Amuktamalyada emphasised the value of improving harbours and treating foreign merchants favourably. Encouraging commerce was not merely a way to make towns wealthy. It also helped rulers obtain horses and other strategic goods that could otherwise reach rival states.

A Gujarat connection: movement of skilled artisans

Commercial connections extended beyond the exchange of finished goods. Skilled artisans also moved between regions. During the 15th century, silk weavers known as Pattanulkars migrated from the Gujarat region to Vijayanagara. This illustrates how medieval regional economies were linked through the movement of people, skills and craft traditions.

The migration should not be confused with a claim that Gujarat was governed by Vijayanagara. It is evidence of interregional economic and cultural connections, rather than direct political control.

Prelims focus

  • Raichur Doab: fertile and strategically contested agricultural region.
  • Kamalapuram tank and Hiriya canal: water-management works associated with Vijayanagara.
  • Kudirai chettis: merchants involved in the horse trade.
  • 1498: Portuguese arrival on India's western coast; 1510: Portuguese capture of Goa.
  • Amuktamalyada: connects the ruler's commercial policy with imported strategic goods.
  • Trap: The migration of Gujarat's Pattanulkar weavers does not imply Vijayanagara's political control over Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, sections 2.1 and 3.1, pp. 172–173 and 177; NIOS, History (315), Lesson 11, discussion of regional trade and artisan migration, p. 175, and sections 11.7–11.8; IGNOU, The Regional Powers: 13th–15th Century, Unit 28, discussion of Bahmani expansion and coastal trade. Online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Agriculture, Commerce, Ports and the Military Economy

body:
The capital's physical setting

Vijayanagara, whose ruins survive at Hampi in Karnataka, was situated in a landscape of granite hills and the Tungabhadra River. The hills provided natural defensive advantages, while the river and artificial waterworks supplied the settlement and its cultivated surroundings.

The capital was more than a royal residence. It contained sacred places, commercial streets, administrative and ceremonial buildings, residential areas, agricultural land and extensive fortifications.

Three major urban areas

The surviving city is commonly understood through 3 broad areas:

  • Sacred centre: The northern area, associated with the Tungabhadra River and important religious sites, including the Virupaksha temple.
  • Urban core: The larger settlement, containing residential and commercial areas, roads, markets, shrines and other facilities.
  • Royal centre: The south-western area, containing important courtly and ceremonial structures, enclosures and temples.

These were functional descriptions rather than completely isolated districts. The royal centre, for example, contained numerous temples, showing that political and religious activities could occupy the same broad area.

Fortifications that protected more than buildings

One of the most distinctive features of Vijayanagara was its system of fortification walls. The 15th-century visitor Abdur Razzaq described 7 lines of fortifications.

These defences surrounded not only buildings but also parts of the surrounding agricultural landscape. This was important because armies besieging a medieval city could attempt to cut off its food supplies. Protecting productive land inside the outer defensive system helped the inhabitants withstand a prolonged siege.

Within the settlement, additional defensive enclosures protected important areas. Guarded gateways controlled entry to the city, while roads connected the gates with markets and ceremonial spaces.

Water supply and irrigation

The rocky environment made careful water management necessary. Streams were dammed or embanked to create reservoirs, while canals carried water to fields and built-up areas.

The Kamalapuram tank supplied nearby agricultural lands and contributed water to the royal centre. The Hiriya canal drew water from the Tungabhadra and irrigated the cultivated valley between the sacred centre and the urban core.

Waterworks performed several connected functions: supplying residents, sustaining agriculture, supporting gardens and helping maintain the capital's economic life.

Markets and everyday urban life

Important roads often extended outward from temple gateways. Along them stood pillared market streets where merchants conducted business. Vijayanagara was known for markets in precious stones, jewellery, cloth, horses and food provisions.

The Portuguese visitor Domingo Paes described the city's markets, gardens and abundant supplies. Other travellers also recorded aspects of its prosperity and buildings. Their accounts help establish that Vijayanagara was a major commercial and urban centre, not only a fortified military capital.

Hampi's surviving monuments form the Group of Monuments at Hampi, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986. This modern recognition concerns the historical and architectural significance of the site.

Prelims focus

  • Hampi: the site of the former Vijayanagara capital in Karnataka.
  • Abdur Razzaq: described 7 lines of fortifications.
  • Kamalapuram tank: irrigation and water supply.
  • Hiriya canal: water drawn from the Tungabhadra system.
  • Domingo Paes: Portuguese account of Vijayanagara's markets and city life.
  • Trap: The fortified area included agricultural land, not only palaces and residences.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, sections 3–4 and 6, pp. 176–180 and 188–191; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Group of Monuments at Hampi', Description and Outstanding Universal Value, including the 1986 inscription (consulted 19 November 2026).]

title: Hampi: Fortifications, Water Systems and Urban Organisation

body:
Why rulers patronised temples

Temples were important religious, social, cultural and economic institutions in medieval South India. They received gifts and land grants, supported festivals and learning, and provided places where rulers displayed their authority.

Vijayanagara's rulers built on earlier architectural traditions associated with dynasties such as the Cholas and Hoysalas. They expanded temples and commissioned monumental gateways, pillared halls and ceremonial structures.

Virupaksha temple and royal authority

The Virupaksha temple at Hampi is associated with Virupaksha, a form of Shiva. Its origins predate Vijayanagara, but it was substantially enlarged under the empire.

Vijayanagara rulers claimed to exercise authority on behalf of Virupaksha. Royal orders were associated with the expression Shri Virupaksha. This connected political legitimacy with a prominent religious institution.

Krishnadeva Raya commissioned a hall at the temple to commemorate his accession and is credited with its eastern gateway. These additions demonstrate how temple architecture could commemorate royal events.

Raya gopurams and mandapas

A gopuram is a monumental gateway tower at a South Indian temple. Under Vijayanagara patronage, exceptionally large gateways became prominent and are often called raya gopurams.

A mandapa is a pillared hall or pavilion. Mandapas could accommodate gatherings and ceremonies. A kalyana mandapa was associated with the ceremonial celebration of a deity's marriage. These structures were often connected by long pillared corridors and temple streets.

Gopuram and mandapa

A gopuram is a gateway tower; a mandapa is a hall or pavilion. They are different architectural elements, even though both may belong to the same temple complex.

Vitthala temple and the stone chariot

The Vitthala temple is associated with Vitthala, a form of Vishnu. The worship of Vitthala was especially associated with Maharashtra, illustrating the movement of religious traditions between regions.

The temple complex is particularly well known for its stone chariot. It is an architectural shrine in the form of a chariot, not an ordinary vehicle used to transport people. The complex also contains pillared halls and other elaborate stone structures.

Religious buildings within the royal centre

The Hazara Rama temple stood in the royal centre and was probably closely associated with the king and his household. Its surviving sculpted panels depict episodes from the Ramayana.

The Lotus Mahal is another important structure in the royal centre. Its arches reflect architectural forms associated with Indo-Islamic building traditions. Its precise original function is not firmly established, although it has been suggested that it may have served as a council chamber.

Mahanavami and the display of royal power

The Mahanavami dibba is a massive raised platform in the royal centre. It is associated with the ceremonial world of Mahanavami or Dussehra, when Vijayanagara rulers displayed their power and received recognition from subordinate chiefs.

Royal ceremonies included processions, displays of horses and elephants, performances and reviews of military forces. Nayakas presented tribute and gifts. These occasions brought together religion, military organisation and political authority. The exact use of every surviving structure during these festivities is not entirely certain, so the platform should not be presented as the proven location of every ceremony.

Painting and artistic traditions

Vijayanagara patronage also supported mural painting. At the Virupaksha temple, paintings in a mandapa depict religious narratives and subjects associated with the ruling tradition. The temple at Lepakshi in present-day Andhra Pradesh preserves important examples of Vijayanagara-period painting.

Characteristics of these murals include faces shown in profile, prominent eyes and expressive outlines. Later Nayaka painting traditions continued and adapted aspects of Vijayanagara artistic practice.

Prelims focus

  • Virupaksha temple: Hampi; associated with Shiva and royal legitimacy.
  • Vitthala temple: associated with Vishnu; famous for its stone chariot.
  • Hazara Rama temple: Ramayana reliefs in the royal centre.
  • Raya gopuram: monumental royal gateway tower.
  • Mahanavami dibba: ceremonial platform associated with royal displays.
  • Trap: The Lotus Mahal's original function is uncertain; its name alone does not establish its use.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, sections 4–5, pp. 180–188; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, 'Later Mural Traditions', pp. 64–66; Archaeological Survey of India, 'Hampi (1986), Karnataka', monument descriptions; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Group of Monuments at Hampi', Description. Online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four distinct Vijayanagara structures and their purposes, with temple patronage linking kingship and religious authority.
pictures.caption: Royal patronage linked temple gateways, ritual spaces and courtly ceremonies.

title: Vijayanagara Architecture, Religious Patronage and Courtly Ceremonies

body:
Gulbarga: the first capital

The Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347 and initially governed from Gulbarga, also called Ahsanabad, in present-day Karnataka. Its buildings demonstrate the importance of fortified cities and royal architectural patronage in the Deccan.

The Gulbarga Fort was a major defensive and administrative centre. The city's Jami Masjid is a significant example of mosque architecture associated with the Bahmani period. The Haft Gumbaz complex is known for royal tombs connected with the early Bahmani rulers.

Bidar: the later Bahmani capital

During the 15th century, the Bahmani capital shifted from Gulbarga to Bidar. Bidar became an important royal, administrative and cultural centre. Its fortifications and monumental buildings reflect the Sultanate's investment in urban defence and courtly prestige.

The Bidar Fort and the Bahmani royal tombs at Ashtur are important surviving reminders of this period.

Mahmud Gawan's madrasa

One of Bidar's best-known monuments is the Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan. A madrasa is an institution for education and scholarly instruction. The building's association with Mahmud Gawan shows that his importance extended beyond military and administrative reform.

The madrasa's architecture included teaching and residential spaces and reflected artistic influences associated with the Persianate world. Decorative tilework is a notable feature of the surviving structure.

Interaction between regional and Persianate traditions

The Bahmani court attracted scholars, administrators and artisans from different regions. Persianate traditions influenced court culture, education and architecture, while local Deccan materials, building practices and artistic preferences also contributed to distinctive regional forms.

Architectural exchange was not confined to one political or religious community. Vijayanagara buildings such as the Lotus Mahal incorporated arches associated with Indo-Islamic traditions, while Deccan Sultanate architecture developed through interaction with regional practices.

Distinguishing Bahmani and later Deccan monuments

MonumentLocationMain association
Jami MasjidGulbargaBahmani capital and religious architecture
Haft GumbazGulbargaEarly Bahmani royal tombs
Mahmud Gawan MadrasaBidarBahmani educational patronage
Bahmani tombs at AshturNear BidarBahmani royal burials
Gol GumbazVijayapura, formerly BijapurLater Adil Shahi Sultanate

The last distinction is important. The Gol Gumbaz at Vijayapura belongs to the Adil Shahi period, after the emergence of Bijapur as a separate Deccan Sultanate. It should not be identified as a monument built by the original Bahmani ruling dynasty.

Gulbarga and Bidar's Bahmani monuments form part of India's Monuments and Forts of the Deccan Sultanate proposal on UNESCO's Tentative List. Tentative-list inclusion is not the same as inscription on the World Heritage List.

Prelims focus

  • Gulbarga: first Bahmani capital; associated with its Jami Masjid and Haft Gumbaz.
  • Bidar: later Bahmani capital.
  • Mahmud Gawan's madrasa: Bidar.
  • Ashtur: associated with Bahmani royal tombs.
  • Gol Gumbaz: Adil Shahi monument at Vijayapura, not an original Bahmani royal monument.
  • Trap: A site on UNESCO's Tentative List is not automatically an inscribed World Heritage Site.

[Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Monuments and Forts of the Deccan Sultanate', India Tentative List submission of 15 April 2014, sections 'Bahmani Monuments at Gulbarga' and 'Bahmani and Barid Shahi Monuments at Bidar'; Government of Karnataka, Bidar District Administration, 'Historical Monuments', sections on the fort and Mahmud Gawan Madrasa; NIOS, History (315), Lesson 11, section 11.7. Online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]
